cards.explanation: The answer is True. The Teacher says, "…one’s day of death is better than his day of birth." (Ecclesiastes 7:1) Yes, he really said it, and no, I did not make my eyebrows go up on purpose. He says it right after the line about a good name, so I'd keep the two together, friends.

The reason is that death comes to every person. The verse says, "…since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:2) So the house of mourning is a place where the living get reminded of something real. I'd rather sit there than be the guy at the feast who's too busy to notice.

The answer is False. The Teacher says, "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure." (Ecclesiastes 7:4) The two hearts are in two different houses. He sorts them out in one short verse, and I respect a man who gets to the point.

The word is "heed." The Teacher says, "It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools." (Ecclesiastes 7:5) Heeding means you take it in and don't just nod. I've nodded at plenty of good advice while thinking about something else, friends, and that's not heeding.

The answer is the laughter of the fool. The Teacher says, "For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:6) Then he adds, "This too is futile." The fool's laughter is the thing that's like those crackling thorns.

The answer is True. The Teacher says, "Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:7) Both warnings sit in one verse, friends. Extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart.

The better one is a patient spirit. The Teacher says, "The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one." (Ecclesiastes 7:8) Patient beats proud. I've waited on a batch to cool while everybody hovered, and I think patience is also what keeps the cookies from breaking.

The word is "fool." The verse says, "Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:9) Anger settles in, like it's found a comfy chair. I'd rather not hand it a seat, friends.

The answer is False. The Teacher tells us not to ask why the old days were better than these. He adds, "For it is unwise of you to ask about this." (Ecclesiastes 7:10) He doesn't say it's wise, friends. He says it's unwise, plain and simple.

The word is "life." The verse says, "For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner." (Ecclesiastes 7:12) Money covers you, and so does wisdom. But only wisdom is said to preserve life.

The word is "straighten." The Teacher says, "Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13) It's a question with no one stepping forward. I'd keep my mustache in my pockets on this one.

The answer is to be joyful. The Teacher says, "In the day of prosperity, be joyful…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) Good days are for joy. I'll happily take that instruction, friends, and I won't need it explained twice.

The answer is True. The verse says, "…consider this: God has made one of these along with the other…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) The two days come as a pair, prosperity and adversity. That's what the Teacher wants us to consider when the hard day shows up.

The reason the text gives is so a man cannot discover what comes after him. The verse says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14) Whatever comes after him, he can't discover it. That's why I keep the ovens ready and leave the schedule to God.
